unrelated members and utility classes. Solid arrows show navigable associations, dashed arrows show

Customers, dogs and activities use persistent IDs as their identities. These IDs are assigned by the
WatchDog and are stored with the records, so they remain stable across application restarts and
are not affected by filtering, list positions or deletion of other records. This allows commands and
relationships to refer to a record reliably even when the visible list changes.
`LinkCommandParser` accepts `c/CUSTOMER_ID d/DOG_ID [DOG_ID]...`: one customer field followed by
one dog field containing distinct, whitespace-separated IDs. Repeated `d/` prefixes are rejected.
`LinkCommand` delegates the batch to `Model.linkDogs`; `ModelManager` forwards to `WatchDog`.
The WatchDog looks up persistent IDs in the complete lists and validates every endpoint and ownership
constraint before publishing one replacement dog list. A rejected batch throws `LinkException` without
changing records or filters; the command translates it to `CommandException` for user feedback.
After successful link or unlink publication, an internal assertion checks that every requested dog ID
still exists and has the intended owner, or no owner for unlink. These checks do not mutate records or
replace the ordinary validation of command input.
Each immutable `Dog` stores an optional owner customer ID. This is the single source of truth;
customers do not store a duplicate dog-ID list. A dog may be unlinked or have one owner, while a customer
may own any number of dogs. Linking an already-owned dog is rejected, including links to the same owner.
Dog equality includes ownership, while identity remains the persistent dog ID.
whitespace-separated dog IDs in one field; repeated dog prefixes and mixed prefixes
are rejected. `UnlinkCommand` delegates to `Model.unlinkCustomerDogs` or `Model.unlinkDogs` and translates
`UnlinkException` into command feedback. `WatchDog` validates every selected dog exists and has an owner
before publishing one replacement list of unowned copies. Dogs may belong to different customers.
The customer form validates the customer, selects all their dogs from the complete list, and uses the
same atomic batch operation. Missing customers and customers with no linked dogs are rejected.
Unlinking preserves records and filters, including a customer's last dog, and uses the existing nullable
`ownerId` storage field without a schema change.
`WatchDog.removeCustomer` clears ownership of that customer's dogs, regardless of filters,
preserving their persistent IDs and details. Unowned dog cards show a person icon followed by `None`.
Removing a dog leaves its customer intact. Customer edits must preserve persistent IDs to keep links valid.
Observable list updates refresh dog cards, which display customer IDs without changing search filters.
Customer cards display owned dog IDs below backup contact. `CustomerListPanel` observes the complete dog list
as well as visible customers, so these IDs remain accurate when dog cards are filtered out.
`JsonAdaptedDog` persists `ownerId`. A missing or null field means unlinked, preserving compatibility
with older files. Negative owner IDs and references to missing customers are rejected on load;
owner IDs must be integer JSON numbers, so fractions and numeric strings cannot silently change ownership.
Customers are restored before dogs. Copies of WatchDog retain ownership through immutable dogs.
The shared model boundaries also reject dangling owner IDs: `setDog` validates the replacement,
`setCustomers` checks that existing owners remain present, and `resetData` validates ownership,
customer-ID uniqueness, and identity counters against snapshots of the incoming data before changing
records. Customer deletion uses its explicit
unlinking path instead of removing a referenced customer through `setCustomers`.
`EditDogCommand` preserves the current owner ID when constructing a replacement dog, so editing details
does not unlink the dog. Ownership changes remain explicit through linking, unlinking, or customer deletion.
Deleting a dog also removes its enrolment records in the same address-book operation, including past
occurrences; other dogs' enrolments and activity schedules are preserved.
Dog participation in an activity occurrence is represented by a separate `Enrolment` record containing
an activity ID, a dog ID, and an occurrence date. This separates the reusable activity schedule from
the dogs attending it while distinguishing occurrences of recurring activities.
It also allows dogs to be enrolled or unenrolled independently without modifying the activity's
schedule or storing duplicate dog objects inside `Activity`.

* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.

* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.

successful command, `MainWindow` captures one date and refreshes both activity panels with it.
There is no midnight scheduler; the date is re-evaluated on the next refresh.

### Removal of the legacy person feature
WatchDog uses customer and dog records. The original AB3 person records, tags, person-only
commands (`add`, `edit`, `delete INDEX` and `find`), person storage adapters and unused list panels
have been removed. Shared components such as `WatchDog`, preferences, parsing utilities,
help, `clear` and JSON storage remain in use.
Existing JSON files may contain a legacy `persons` field. It is ignored on loading and omitted
on the next save; its records are not converted to customers. Customer/dog records, activity schedules,
dated enrolments, ownership links and all three persistent-ID counters are preserved. A file containing only
legacy persons loads as an empty WatchDog book. No startup sample person records are created.

Customer names support Unicode letters, combining marks, and slashes. `ArgumentTokenizer` treats
space-prefixed `n/`, `p/`, `e/`, and `bc/` as field delimiters, so these sequences cannot be entered
literally within a name through `addcustomer` or `editcustomer`. Other sequences, such as `s/o` and
`d/o`, remain name text. `Name` normalizes stored names to Unicode NFC, and
`CustomerSearchPredicate` applies the same normalization to names and search queries before matching.
`Email` validates a nonempty local part made of English letters, digits, and `+`, `_`, `.`, `'`, or `-`.
Its regex accepts dot-separated nonempty atoms: supported non-dot punctuation may start or end an atom
or repeat, while leading, trailing, and consecutive dots are rejected. Other punctuation and quoted
local parts remain unsupported. Adding, editing, and loading customers share this validation;
email searches match the stored value ignoring case. The domain regex permits one or more nonempty
dot-separated labels, including single-label domains. Each label starts and ends with an ASCII letter
or digit; internal hyphens must be single, and the final label has at least two characters.
Consecutive hyphens (including the `xn--` prefix of punycode labels) are unsupported.

On `undo`, `LogicManager` captures the current state for redo, restores the undo snapshot, moves
the history slots, then saves WatchDog. `redo` symmetrically captures the current state for
undo, restores the redo snapshot, moves the slots, and saves. An ordinary command updates history

of retaining in-memory changes when a save fails: the corresponding inverse remains available,
and `clear` still invalidates history. A failed write to the temporary file leaves the saved state intact;
a file system without atomic moves uses regular replacement and cannot guarantee atomicity during replacement.

accepted by `addcustomer` can be searched without ambiguity. Quotes are removed before matching.

lowercase fields `n/`, `p/`, `e/`, `d/`, `bc/`, and `i/`. Names are normalised for case-insensitive substring
matching, while contact numbers and email addresses use exact matching. Multiple dog IDs are parsed from

matched exactly against existing customer IDs.

searches are rejected. The parser removes spaces and hyphens and converts `+65` followed by
eight digits to local form before creating the command. Other international numbers retain
their leading `+`. Consequently, `searchc p/+65 9123-4567` matches a stored `91234567`.
An invalid contact query, including a `+65` number with seven or nine following digits, fails
before the command executes and leaves all current filters unchanged.

NFR-01. **Platform compatibility**: Should work on any _mainstream OS_ as long as it has Java `25` or above installed.
NFR-02. **Offline operation**: After installation and setup, all core dog and customer management operations shall work without an internet connection.

NFR-03. **Performance**: With up to 500 dog records and 500 customer records, WatchDog shall display the result of a dog or customer add, edit, delete, or search command, or `reset`, within 2 seconds of submission on the agreed test laptop.
NFR-04. **Startup time**: With the same dataset, WatchDog shall load its saved records and become ready to accept commands within 10 seconds of launch on the agreed test laptop.
NFR-05. **Keyboard usability**: After launch, users shall be able to perform all core dog and customer management operations using the keyboard without requiring mouse interaction.

NFR-06. **Typing efficiency**: A user with above average typing speed for regular English text (i.e. not code, not system admin commands) should be able to accomplish most of the tasks faster using commands than using the mouse.

NFR-07. **Error clarity**: For invalid command syntax, missing required fields, or invalid field values, WatchDog shall display an English error message identifying the problem. Missing-field errors shall also show the relevant command format.

NFR-08. **Robustness**: An invalid command or an input that fails validation shall not terminate the application or change existing records. The application shall remain ready to accept the next command.
NFR-09. **Data persistence**: Following successful data changes and a normal application exit, WatchDog shall restore the updated dog records, customer records and their associations when reopened.
NFR-10. **Privacy**: WatchDog shall store dog and customer records locally and shall not transmit their contents to external services.
* **WatchDog**: The application used to manage a dog daycare centre's customer and dog information.
* **User**: The person operating WatchDog, primarily the dog daycare manager.
* **Customer**: A person whose contact details are recorded because they use the daycare's services for their dog or dogs.
* **Dog record**: The information stored about an individual dog, including its ID, name, breed and size.
* **Customer record**: The information stored about a customer, including their ID, name, primary phone number, email and backup contact.
* **Dog ID**: A unique integer assigned by WatchDog to identify a dog record. Dogs with the same name are distinguished by their IDs.
* **Customer ID**: A unique integer assigned by WatchDog to identify a customer record. Customers with the same name are distinguished by their IDs.
* **List position**: A record's position in the currently displayed list. Unlike a record ID, this position may change when the list is filtered or reordered.
* **Ownership**: The recorded relationship indicating which customer owns a dog.
* **Primary phone number**: The customer's main telephone number, used as the first contact option.
* **Backup contact**: An alternative telephone number used when the customer cannot be reached through their primary phone number.
* **Breed**: The recorded breed or breed mix of a dog, such as Chihuahua, Shiba Inu or a mixed breed.
* **Size**: A user-selected category for a dog: small, medium, large or giant. WatchDog does not infer
this category from weight or enforce weight thresholds.
* **Activity**: A reusable schedule for a care task, such as feeding, grooming or exercise. Dogs are booked into its dated occurrences through enrolments.
* **Activity ID**: A unique integer assigned by WatchDog to identify an activity schedule. It remains stable across application restarts.
* **Recurrence**: The rule determining whether an activity occurs once, daily or weekly.
* **Occurrence**: A date on which an activity takes place according to its start date and recurrence.
* **Enrolment**: A dated booking for a dog in an activity occurrence. It does not indicate actual attendance or check-in.

WatchDog is a desktop application that helps dog daycare managers manage customers, dogs, ownership relationships, and activity schedules. It combines keyboard commands with a JavaFX graphical interface and stores records locally.

Alongside implementation, I took an active role in coordinating the team's work, clarifying product decisions, and supporting teammates with technical questions. My main implementation contributions were activity creation and persistence, customer-dog linking and unlinking, and daycare statistics, with additional work on code quality, testing, and UI integration.
Given below are my contributions to the project.
* **New feature: Activity schedules and the `addactivity` command**

* **Related PRs:** [#93](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/93) (model, creation, recurrence, and persistence); [#127](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/127) (restoration consistency and boundary tests); [#145](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/145) (parser refactoring and command contracts); [#177](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/177) (positive activity IDs).
* **What it does:** Creates activities with a name, date, start and end times, and recurrence rule. Activities have persistent IDs and can be saved and restored across application sessions.

* **Why it matters:** Managers can define reusable schedules instead of repeatedly entering the same activity. This provides the scheduling foundation used by the team's enrolment and activity-management features.

* **Design and coordination challenge:** Our team discussions established the intended final activity view, while the underlying model design and implementation were my responsibility. Activities differed substantially from customer and dog records: they needed time ranges, recurrence rules, and support for dated bookings. I had to translate the agreed user-facing view into a model structure and API before teammates could build their commands on it. This required planning how the parts would fit together, since later interface changes could affect several teammates and require coordinated rework.

* **Implementation highlights:** Implemented immutable activity schedules and supporting value types, recurrence calculations, command parsing and validation, model integration, and JSON storage. Kept schedule rules in the activity model, input syntax in the parser, and persistent identity allocation in the model operation. Invalid creation requests do not consume an activity ID.

* **Technical challenges:** Calculated recurring occurrences on demand, including start-date and date-range boundaries, without storing an unbounded list of future dates. Preserved the next unused ID across reloads and rejected fractional or textual JSON IDs before automatic conversion could hide invalid input.

* **Recurrence design decision:** Chose one stored schedule per recurring series, with separate bookings identified by activity ID, dog ID, and occurrence date. This avoids generating unlimited future records or maintaining an arbitrary booking horizon, while allowing dogs to be booked independently for each occurrence. I also helped define the edit and deletion rules for teammates implementing those commands: a series with enrolments cannot be edited, and deleting a series removes its associated bookings. These rules keep references consistent without requiring booking migration or per-occurrence schedule exceptions, at the cost of less flexible editing and removal of past bookings when a series is deleted.
* **Integration improvement: Consistent restoration of activities and bookings**

* **Related PRs:** [#127](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/127) (notification ordering); [#205](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/205) (snapshot validation and boundary tests).
* **What it does:** Validates incoming snapshots before replacing live records and restores activity schedules together with their associated enrolments.
* **Why it matters:** Loading or restoring related data must preserve valid references and give observers a consistent view of the restored schedules and bookings.

* **Technical challenges:** JavaFX listeners can run midway through restoration and observe new schedules with old bookings or counters. I ordered updates and batched activity notifications so listeners see consistent activity and enrolment data. Validating snapshots in an isolated candidate model also prevents invalid bookings from partially replacing live data. Tests check both the restored values and what listeners observe during updates.

* **Related PRs:** [#83](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/83) (commands, model/storage integration, and ownership display); [#155](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/155), [#205](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/205) (ownership invariants); [#177](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/177) (space-separated dog IDs).
* **What it does:** Links multiple dogs to a customer in one command. Removes ownership links by dog IDs or customer ID while retaining the underlying customer and dog records.
* **Why it matters:** Managers can maintain ownership information separately from record creation and deletion, including handling customers with several dogs and dogs without an assigned owner.

* **Implementation highlights:** Added model-level ownership checks and integrated relationship information into customer and dog cards. My contribution to these shared components focused on ownership relationships and their display.

* **Technical challenges:** A missing or already-owned dog must reject the entire batch, even if earlier dogs are valid. I prepared replacements separately and published them only after every check passed, using persistent IDs independently of display filters. Ownership checks also protect model replacement and restoration paths that bypass command parsing.

* **Related PRs:** [#144](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/144) (command and reusable enrolment query); [#145](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/145), [#205](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/205) (contracts and boundary tests); [#220](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T15-4/tp/pull/220) (persistence/history integration tests and manual-testing guidance).
* **What it does:** Shows customer and dog totals, total activity schedules, schedules with an occurrence today or later, today's activities, and distinct dogs enrolled today.
* **Why it matters:** Gives managers an overview of their records and today's bookings without manually counting across lists or changing the current view.

* **Implementation highlights:** Counts from the full model regardless of active filters and preserves records, filters, selection, and undo/redo history. Added a reusable model query for the distinct dogs enrolled on a supplied date.

* **Technical challenges:** Distinguished schedule counts from dated bookings and deduplicated dogs by persistent ID, including dogs with identical names.
